Block/procedural programming is fine too, you just have to do a little more work. For example, instead of an Enemy class that you subclass into more specific types that implement versions of the same abstract calls, you'd have an Enemy record with some bookkeeping for the kind of enemy it is and then some switch statements to vary behavior based on that kind.

It's actually not that much more work (for games) and basically implements what a run-time library would actually do. It was the predominant programming strategy for games well into the late 80s and early 90s due to it's performance, tweakability, and low code and memory footprint compared to a fully-featured dynamic typing system. Even in the 90s, anything OOP was there only to make some boilerplate stuff easier while casting and resolving stuff in game loop itself would murder performance. Until about the PSX era, when console manufacturers actually started shipping libraries with their dev kits (as opposed to just big hardware technical manuals), almost all console games were written in this way.
